newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-SAS flags arrival of tough times.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-SAS flags arrival of tough times.

text.p: Scandinavian Airlines Systems (SAS) on Monday reported a 31 percent slump in 1996 profits and warned that competition was likely to get even tougher in Scandinavian skies in 1997.

"The report looks poor and is in line with our sell recommendation on the share," Finn Bjarke Petersen, analyst at Aros Securities in Copenhagen, said after the figures were released showing earnings were a little better than analyst forecasts.
The airline, owned by the governments of Denmark, Norway and Sweden and private investors, reported a pre-tax profit of 1.82 billion crowns ($246 million) for 1996.
The profit was above a company forecast of 1.74 billion crowns made in mid-November and above an average market prediction of 1.72 billion crowns.
The SAS share price rose one crown to 96.5 in Stockholm even though analysts said the airline's figures had been distorted by exchange rates used.
They said SAS had upgraded figures for the first nine months of the year by using a different average currency rate in its year-end report than in its nine-month report.
"It's wrong to connect historical figures with real foreign exchange rates," one analyst said.
In November, SAS said its nine-month pre-tax profit amounted to 1.26 billion crowns. Adding a fourth quarter profit of 365 million crowns gives a full-year profit of around 1.63 billion crowns.
Analysts pointed out that the fourth quarter of 1996 was weaker than the corresponding quarter a year earlier when the company posted a profit of 487 million crowns.
And the company forecast for the future was downbeat. With eight new airlines entering SAS's market in 1996, the company predicted that competition would get tougher.
"Competition in the airline industry is expected...to intensify further in 1997 which could lead to big over-capacity putting pressure on prices and revenue," the airline said in a statement.
SAS said it would aim to hold this year's earnings at around the 1996 level and that it was working on certain areas to try to avoid its performance deteriorating further.

"We see a number of factors that can make 1997 tougher than we thought when we laid down our budgets," SAS managing director Jan Stenberg told a news conference. "Our ambition will have to be to hold at 1996's result.
"A productivity programme can give us improved finances, increased revenue and reduced costs."
Analysts were not impressed, however. with Petersen saying: "Those are just general statements."
Another Copenhagen-based analyst agreed, saying: "Volumes will increase by five-seven percent but costs will increase at a faster pace while prices and capacity utilisation will fall."
The Danish analysts did not expect SAS to be able to counteract these negative trends and added that the airline's statements showed it was under pressure.

Analysts also said there was a lot of talk about alliances between ailrineds but not enough about earnings. Last year the airline started a strategic cooperation with Lufthansa, United Airlines and Thai Airways International.

It was last week named among a group of nine airlines said by industry sources to be forming an alliance to counteract a planned link-up between British Airways and American Airlines. ($ = 7.394 Swedish Crowns)
